title: A headache after the festival: fever, headache and neck stiffness in an 18-year-old woman in general practice
desc: In this station the candidate takes a focused headache history from Molly, an 18-year-old university student seen in general practice, and does a focused examination. She came home from a three-day music festival recently. She had a runny nose 3 days ago, and since yesterday evening she has had a worsening, generalised throbbing headache with fever, neck stiffness and photophobia. She has no rash. In Part 2 the candidate first reads her observations, gives an ISBAR handover to the ED, makes the diagnosis and plans emergency management in general practice, including notifying public health. They are then given her CSF and blood results from the hospital, which confirm meningococcal meningitis. They plan definitive treatment, clearance antibiotics for her close contacts through public health, and safety netting for those contacts.
focus: Recognising bacterial meningitis from a fever-and-headache history, giving parenteral antibiotics and arranging emergency transfer from general practice, interpreting CSF, and protecting close contacts of a patient with meningococcal disease
diagnosis: Bacterial meningitis due to Neisseria meningitidis (meningococcal meningitis)
stem: You are a final-year medical student on placement in a metropolitan general practice. Your next patient is Molly, an 18-year-old university student who has recently come home from a music festival. Since late yesterday she has had a constant headache and has felt generally unwell. Your GP supervisor will see her after you.
tasks: Take a focused history from Molly and perform a focused examination, telling the examiner what you are examining (10 minutes).

The examiner will give you Molly's observations, and later her lumbar puncture and blood results from the hospital. Interpret them, then outline your management approach and safety netting (5 minutes).
patient:
Role: You are Molly, an 18-year-old first-year university student. You feel awful: hot, achy and exhausted, with a pounding head. You sit hunched with your eyes half-closed because the light hurts, and you move your head as little as possible. You answer clearly and sensibly (you are not confused), but you speak quietly and slowly. Your mum drove you here and is waiting in the waiting room. The examiner gives the examination findings below when the candidate says what they are examining.

Opening line: “I’ve had this headache since last night and it just keeps getting worse. I feel terrible.”

The headache (give only when asked):

  • Site: all over your head. You can’t point to one spot, and it doesn’t spread anywhere.
  • Onset: it started yesterday evening. It came on over a few hours, not suddenly, and it did not hit you like a blow to the head.
  • Character: throbbing, and constant since it started.
  • Course: it has been getting steadily worse since last night.
  • Severity: 8 out of 10.
  • What helps: nothing. You took paracetamol (1 g last night and 1 g this morning) and it didn’t help.
  • What makes it worse: looking at lights and moving your head.
  • Impact: you couldn’t sleep last night and you can’t do your university work.

Other symptoms (give each only when asked):

  • Cold symptoms: a runny nose that started 3 days ago, while you were at the festival.
  • Fever: yes. Your mum checked your temperature last night and it was 38.5 °C.
  • Neck: yes, your neck is stiff and sore, especially when you look down.
  • Light: yes, bright light hurts your eyes.
  • Tiredness: yes, you are exhausted and achy all over.

Say no if asked about:

  • a rash, spots or bruises anywhere (you haven’t noticed any);
  • confusion, drowsiness or feeling “not with it”; seizures or fits;
  • weakness, numbness, trouble speaking or changes in your vision;
  • nausea or vomiting; dizziness or a spinning feeling; any change in your walking or balance;
  • a head injury or fall; a sudden headache like a thunderclap;
  • headaches like this before; flashing lights or zigzags before the headache; a red or watering eye on one side with the pain; a tight band around your head; sharp pain in your face set off by touch or chewing; jaw pain when chewing or a tender scalp;
  • problems with your immune system, or steroids or other medicines that lower your immunity.

Past medical history: none. You have never been in hospital.

Vaccinations (when asked): “I think I had all my school ones, but I’m not sure about the meningococcal ones. Mum might know.” If asked specifically about the meningococcal ACWY or B vaccines: you are not sure whether you had them.

Medicines: nothing regular. Paracetamol for this headache, as above. You don’t take the pill.

Allergies: none that you know of.

Family history: your grandfather had a stroke at 60. Nothing else.

Social history:

  • The festival (give the details when asked about it): a 3-day music festival with huge crowds; you came home 2 days ago. You camped with three friends and shared a tent with them. You shared drinks with your friends and with people you met there. If asked whether you kissed anyone: no.
  • Alcohol: you drink socially, a few drinks at the festival, and you never binge.
  • Smoking and drugs: you don’t smoke or vape, and you don’t use recreational drugs.
  • Home: you live with your parents. You were born in Australia and haven’t travelled overseas.
  • Lifestyle: you are active and eat a healthy diet.

Ideas, concerns and expectations:

  • Idea: “I thought I was just tired from the festival, but now I’m not sure.”
  • Concern: that it might be something more than tiredness, and that you are falling behind with your university work.
  • Expectation: something stronger for the headache, and a certificate for university.

Question to raise near the end of Part 1: “Is this just a bad flu from the festival?” Accept an honest, brief answer, or a promise to come back to it.

How you change: through Part 1 you stay alert and the headache stays the same. You wince and say “Ow, my neck” when the candidate bends your head forward. No rash appears.

Exam findings (examiner: give only when the candidate says what they are examining):

  • General inspection: unwell and flushed, sitting hunched with her eyes half-closed against the light. She holds her head still. Alert and oriented to time, place and person, with normal speech. GCS 15 (E4 V5 M6).
  • Observations: the practice nurse took them on arrival. Temperature 39.0 °C, HR 124/min regular, BP 112/70 mmHg, RR 24/min, SpO2 97% on room air, capillary refill 2 seconds, capillary glucose 5.4 mmol/L. (The full set, with a repeat, is handed over in Part 2.)
  • Skin (whole body, including trunk, limbs, palms, soles and conjunctivae): no rash, petechiae or purpura. There are no spots to test with a glass. Peripheries warm.
  • Meningism: neck stiffness: resists passive neck flexion and cannot touch her chin to her chest because of pain. Kernig’s sign positive on both sides. Brudzinski’s sign positive (if tested).
  • Fundoscopy: optic discs pink with sharp margins. No papilloedema. No haemorrhages.
  • Pupils and cranial nerves: pupils 4 mm, equal and reactive to light. Visual fields full. Eye movements full with no double vision or nystagmus. Face symmetrical, facial sensation normal. The other cranial nerves are normal.
  • Limbs: no pronator drift. Tone, power (5/5), reflexes and sensation normal and symmetrical. Plantars flexor. Coordination normal.
  • Gait (if tested): walks normally but slowly.
  • Ears, nose and throat: clear nasal discharge with mild congestion. Throat mildly red, with no exudate. Tympanic membranes normal. Sinuses not tender. No significant neck lymph nodes.
  • Chest and heart (if examined): chest clear. Heart sounds dual with no murmur.
  • Temporal arteries (if examined): normal, not tender.

check.x: Professionalism
Performs hand hygiene, introduces self and role, confirms Molly's identity, explains the examination and gains consent (credit also for any accommodation of her photophobia, e.g. dimming the lights).
check.d: Dimming the lights is not required for this mark.

check.x: Acknowledges how unwell she feels, keeps the questions focused because of her pain, asks about alcohol, drugs and festival contacts without judgement, and conveys urgency honestly without alarming her.
History
Characterises the headache:

kids.x: Site and onset: all over and cannot be localised; started yesterday evening and came on over hours, not suddenly.
kids.d: Award only if the speed of onset is specifically asked about.

kids.x: Character, severity and course: throbbing, constant, 8/10, steadily getting worse; no radiation.
Aggravating and relieving factors: paracetamol does not help; worse with lights and moving her head.
Impact: cannot sleep or do her university work.

check.x: Asks about a prodrome and systemic symptoms: runny nose 3 days ago, fever of 38.5 °C at home last night, fatigue and aches.
check.d: Award only if fever is specifically asked about.

check.x: Asks specifically about neck stiffness and photophobia [both present].
Asks specifically about a rash (spots or bruises), linking it to meningococcal disease [none].
Screens for red flags and rules out other causes of headache:
check.d: Award each kid for the cluster asked about.

kids.x: Encephalitis or a complication: confusion, drowsiness, behaviour change or seizures [none].
Subarachnoid haemorrhage and trauma: thunderclap onset, head injury [none].
Raised intracranial pressure or a space-occupying lesion: nausea or vomiting, focal weakness, numbness, speech or visual change, dizziness or change in gait [none].
Primary headaches: previous similar headaches, aura (migraine), one-sided red watering eye (cluster), band-like pain (tension-type) [none].
kids.d: Award for at least two. Also credit asking about jaw claudication (GCA) or triggered facial pain (trigeminal neuralgia).

check.x: Takes the past medical and medication history: no illnesses or admissions; not immunosuppressed; no regular medicines; paracetamol for this headache.
check.d: Award only if immunosuppression is asked about.

check.x: Asks about her vaccination history, specifically the meningococcal vaccines [unsure whether she had meningococcal ACWY or B].
Asks about allergies, particularly to antibiotics [none known].
Takes a family history: grandfather had a stroke at 60.
Takes a social history:

kids.x: The festival and close contacts: 3 days of crowds, home 2 days ago, shared a tent with three friends, shared drinks; no kissing.
kids.d: Award only if the candidate asks who she was in close contact with.

kids.x: Alcohol, smoking and drugs: social drinking with no binges, non-smoker, no recreational drugs.
Home and background: lives with her parents, university student, born in Australia, no overseas travel.

check.x: Explores ideas, concerns and expectations: thought she was tired from the festival but is now unsure, worried about falling behind at university, wants stronger pain relief and a certificate.
Examination
General inspection and conscious state: unwell, flushed, photophobic; alert and oriented, GCS 15.
Asks for the full set of observations, including temperature, HR, BP, RR, SpO2, capillary refill and glucose [T 39.0 °C, HR 124, RR 24, BP 112/70, SpO2 97%, CRT 2 s, BGL 5.4].
check.d: Award for temperature, HR, BP, RR and SpO2; capillary refill and glucose are credit, not required.

check.x: Inspects the whole skin for a petechial or purpuric rash, and states they would do a glass test on any spots [no rash].
check.d: Award only if the trunk and limbs are both inspected.

check.x: Examines for meningism: neck stiffness and Kernig's or Brudzinski's sign [neck stiffness, Kernig's positive].
Performs fundoscopy, looking for papilloedema [none].
Screens for a focal deficit: pupils, cranial nerves, pronator drift, limb power, reflexes and plantars [all normal].
Looks for a source or another cause: ears, throat, sinuses and chest [mild coryza only].
Interpretation

Interprets the observations: fever 39.0 rising to 39.3 °C, tachycardia 124 rising to 130, tachypnoea 24 to 26, BP maintained but falling (112/70 to 108/66), SpO2 and capillary refill normal, alert. States that fever, tachycardia and tachypnoea with suspected CNS infection mean suspected sepsis, worsening over 15 minutes, not yet shocked; with meningism this is an emergency, not a routine review.
check.d: Accept 'possible sepsis', 'suspected sepsis' or 'septic picture'. Award only if the worsening trend is recognised.

check.x: Gives suspected bacterial meningitis, most likely meningococcal, as the most likely diagnosis before the CSF results, justified by fever, a worsening headache, neck stiffness, photophobia and a positive Kernig's sign in an 18-year-old after a festival with uncertain meningococcal vaccination; states that the absence of a rash does not exclude meningococcal disease.
Names differentials, each with a feature for or against from this case: viral meningitis, encephalitis, subarachnoid haemorrhage, migraine, influenza or another viral illness.
check.d: Award for at least three, including encephalitis or subarachnoid haemorrhage, each justified.

check.x: Interprets the CSF:

kids.x: Turbid, with a raised opening pressure (35 cmH2O), a neutrophil-predominant pleocytosis (8500 x10^6/L), high protein (1.1 g/L), low glucose (1.2 mmol/L) and a CSF:serum glucose ratio of 0.24: bacterial meningitis.
kids.d: Award only if the neutrophils, protein and glucose (or ratio) are all interpreted. The turbidity and opening pressure are supporting detail and not required for the mark. No xanthochromia and only 5 red cells argue against SAH; supporting detail, not required. Also credit, not required: the bloods (neutrophilia and a high CRP fit bacterial infection; normal platelets and clotting, so no DIC).

kids.x: Gram-negative diplococci on Gram stain and Neisseria meningitidis PCR detected: meningococcal meningitis; the culture has no growth to date, most likely because the antibiotic was given before the LP; PCR confirms.

check.x: Management
Treats this as an emergency in general practice: calls 000 for an urgent ambulance to the ED, does not let her mum drive her, and does not delay transfer for tests.

Gives a parenteral antibiotic immediately, after checking allergies: benzylpenicillin 2.4 g IV or IM (eTG adult dose; accept 1.2 g per CDNA) or ceftriaxone 2 g IV or IM; does not delay it to take blood cultures or wait for the ambulance.
check.d: Accept either drug with an IV or IM route. Do not award if antibiotics are left until hospital.

check.x: Supports her while waiting: IV access (or IM if access fails), blood cultures only if they do not delay the antibiotic, repeat observations every 15 minutes, oxygen if hypoxic, an IV fluid bolus if signs of shock develop, stays with her, and uses a surgical mask and droplet precautions.

Gives a structured ISBAR phone handover to the ED registrar, including the antibiotic given or being given now (drug and dose), and states a letter with the drug, dose and time will go with her (credit the letter in question 1 or 3).

Explains to Molly in plain words, and offers to bring her mum in, that she may have a serious infection of the lining of the brain, why she needs an antibiotic injection now and why she needs an ambulance rather than a car.
States the definitive treatment for Molly: IV ceftriaxone (2 g 12-hourly), 5 days in total, with no separate clearance antibiotic needed (ceftriaxone clears carriage).
check.d: Award for IV ceftriaxone, 5 days in total, and no separate clearance antibiotic needed; the dose is credit, not required. Optional context only, not required: if the isolate is penicillin-susceptible, benzylpenicillin 2.4 g IV 4-hourly is an alternative, but then she needs a clearance antibiotic before discharge; dexamethasone 10 mg IV 6-hourly is ideally given before or with the first antibiotic dose (Molly had a pre-hospital dose, so the ED team decides according to eTG and local guidance) and is stopped if a non-pneumococcal organism is confirmed.

check.x: Notifies the local public health unit urgently by phone, without waiting for confirmation.
check.d: Score from question 3 (or from the Recommendation in question 1).

check.x: Plans for close contacts through public health: household (her parents) and household-like contacts in the 7 days before she fell ill, such as the friends who shared her tent, receive clearance antibiotics as soon as possible (ciprofloxacin 500 mg orally once, ceftriaxone 250 mg IM once, or rifampicin 600 mg orally 12-hourly for 2 days); MenACWY vaccine for close contacts if the serogroup is A, C, W or Y; MenB vaccine for contacts only if the public health unit advises it.
check.d: Accept one regimen without the dose. Award only if the tent-mates are identified as contacts. Accept "the friends she slept in the same tent with" or "household-like contacts at the festival". The vaccine detail is not required for the mark.

check.x: Safety netting

Gives the close contacts at least three red flags in plain words (fever, severe headache, stiff neck, vomiting, drowsiness or confusion, a rash of spots or bruises that don't fade) and tells them to call 000 or go straight to the ED.
check.d: Award for at least three warning signs in plain words and 000 or the ED named. Also credit, not required: explaining that clearance antibiotics do not fully remove the risk.

check.x: Mentions follow-up for Molly after discharge: a formal hearing test, GP review of her recovery, or a check and update of her meningococcal vaccination.

part2.lead: Here are Molly's observations from the practice nurse: the set taken when she arrived, and a repeat taken 15 minutes later while you were with her. I will give you her hospital results before the last question.
part2.patient:
Molly speaks during the management answer (question 3):

  • When the candidate says she needs to go to hospital: “Can’t Mum just drive me? It’s only 15 minutes away.” Accept the ambulance once the candidate explains kindly and clearly why.
  • When an injection is mentioned: “What’s the injection for? Can’t I just wait until I get to hospital?”

Before question 4, the examiner hands over the hospital results and gives Molly's question as the lead-in: “Before she left, Molly asked you: ‘Is it meningococcal? Are Mum and my friends going to catch it?’”

handover.label: Observations (practice nurse, today)
handover.result: Taken in the treatment room on arrival and repeated 15 minutes later. Molly is seated, on room air.
handover.model:
• Read: at 10:20: temperature 39.0 °C, HR 124 and regular, RR 24, BP 112/70, SpO2 97% on room air, CRT 2 s, alert, glucose 5.4, pain 8/10. At 10:35: temperature 39.3 °C, HR 130, RR 26, BP 108/66, SpO2 97%, alert. The nurse is concerned.
  • Zones (NSW adult Between the Flags chart; check the current CEC version): HR 124 and 130 are in the yellow zone (120–139) in both sets. Temperature 39.0 and 39.3 °C are in the yellow zone (38.5 or above) in both sets. RR 26 at 10:35 is in the yellow zone (25–29); RR 24 at 10:20 is just below it. BP, SpO2 and conscious state are outside the yellow and red zones. Several yellow-zone criteria plus nurse concern call for an urgent clinical review and escalation; in a GP room, with fever and meningism, the response is an emergency ambulance through 000, not observation.
  • For Molly: fever, tachycardia and tachypnoea with suspected CNS infection: suspected sepsis, worsening over 15 minutes, not yet shocked. Her BP is maintained, her perfusion is normal and she is alert.
  • What it changes: give a parenteral antibiotic now and transfer by ambulance. Repeat the observations every 15 minutes while waiting.

rows.note: On arrival; seated, shielding her eyes from the light
Repeat set; nurse concerned, GP informed

handover.label: Lumbar puncture: CSF results (hospital ED, 13:10)
handover.result: CSF collected in the ED at 13:10, with Molly lying on her side, L3/4, three tubes. Opening pressure measured at the procedure. Paired serum glucose taken at 13:05. Clinical details: parenteral antibiotic given in general practice about 2.5 hours before the LP.
handover.model:
• Read: turbid CSF with a raised opening pressure (35 cmH2O). Neutrophils 8500 x10^6/L with 80 lymphocytes: a marked neutrophil-predominant pleocytosis. Protein high (1.1 g/L). Glucose low (1.2 mmol/L); paired with the serum glucose of 5.0 the ratio is 0.24 (1.2/5.0 = 0.24, below 0.4), which strongly suggests bacterial infection. No xanthochromia and only 5 red cells. Gram-negative diplococci on Gram stain; culture has no growth to date; N. meningitidis PCR detected.
  • For Molly: this is acute bacterial meningitis caused by Neisseria meningitidis, which fits her age and the festival. The culture has no growth to date, most likely because the antibiotic was given before the LP; pre-hospital antibiotics often sterilise cultures, so PCR confirms the diagnosis. Without xanthochromia and with almost no red cells, this is not a subarachnoid haemorrhage. The CSF is not viral: in viral meningitis the cells are mainly lymphocytes and the glucose is near normal.
  • What it changes: IV ceftriaxone 2 g 12-hourly, 5 days in total. Public health should already have been notified by phone when meningococcal disease was suspected. Make sure the unit has the laboratory confirmation so that contact tracing and clearance antibiotics go ahead without delay.

labs.title: CSF: appearance, pressure, biochemistry and cell count

rows.n: Paired serum glucose collected 13:05: see blood results

handover.label: Blood results (hospital ED)
handover.result: Bloods collected in the ED at 11:40; glucose collected at 13:05 with the lumbar puncture. Blood cultures (2 sets, 11:40): no growth to date. Neisseria meningitidis PCR (blood): to follow. IV ceftriaxone 2 g 12-hourly charted in the ED.
handover.model:
• Read: WCC 21.6 with neutrophils 19.2 and CRP 168: a marked bacterial inflammatory response. Venous lactate mildly raised at 2.4. Hb, platelets, INR and APTT normal. Sodium, potassium, urea and creatinine normal. Serum glucose 5.0, paired with the CSF glucose of 1.2 (ratio 0.24). Blood cultures have no growth so far, and the PCR is pending.
  • For Molly: the bloods support bacterial sepsis with meningitis. Normal platelets and clotting show no DIC, and with no rash or shock there is no sign yet of fulminant meningococcal septicaemia, but she remains septic and needs close monitoring. Normal clotting also meant the lumbar puncture was safe to do. The raised lactate fits sepsis and needs repeating.
  • What it changes: it gives the serum glucose to pair with the CSF glucose, and a baseline for monitoring (lactate, sodium, renal function, clotting). Blood PCR and cultures may add the serogroup. (Credit only; not a separate mark.)

ask: You are now calling the emergency department registrar at the local hospital to arrange Molly's transfer. Please give an ISBAR handover of Molly, including your interpretation of her observations.
What is your most likely diagnosis, and what else would you consider? Justify your answer.
Outline your management of Molly now, here in general practice.
The next day, the hospital has sent you Molly's lumbar puncture and blood results. Interpret these results, and tell me what happens next for Molly and her close contacts.
expect:
• Identify: medical student at the practice; Molly, 18.
  • Situation: suspected bacterial meningitis, probably meningococcal; she is getting worse; ambulance called; requesting urgent ED review.
  • Background: home 2 days from a festival (shared a tent with three friends); runny nose 3 days ago; fever 38.5 °C last night; headache since yesterday evening; previously well; not immunosuppressed; meningococcal vaccination uncertain; no known allergies.
  • Assessment: T 39.0 rising to 39.3 °C, HR 124 to 130, RR 24 to 26, BP 112/70 to 108/66, SpO2 97% on room air, CRT 2 s: suspected sepsis, worsening, not yet shocked. GCS 15, neck stiffness, Kernig's positive, no rash, normal fundi, no focal signs.
  • Recommendation: antibiotic given or being given now (drug, dose, time); please expect her for cultures, LP and IV antibiotics; public health to be notified.

Most likely: bacterial meningitis, probably meningococcal. For: fever, worsening headache, neck stiffness, photophobia, Kernig's sign, tachycardia; age 18, festival crowds, shared tent, uncertain vaccination. No rash does not exclude it.

  • Viral meningitis: for: coryzal prodrome, alert. Against: she looks septic; cannot be told apart without CSF.
  • Encephalitis: against: alert, oriented, no seizures or focal signs.
  • Subarachnoid haemorrhage: for: photophobia and neck stiffness. Against: gradual onset, fever.
  • Migraine: for: throbbing, photophobia. Against: first ever, fever, meningism.
  • Influenza or other viral illness: for: coryza, fever. Against: meningism.

1. Emergency: call 000 for an ambulance; not the family car; no delay for tests.
  2. Antibiotic now: check allergies (none); benzylpenicillin 2.4 g IV or IM (eTG adult dose; accept 1.2 g per CDNA), or ceftriaxone 2 g IV or IM. Blood cultures only if they do not delay it.
  3. While waiting: IV access, observations every 15 minutes, oxygen if hypoxic, fluid bolus if shocked; stay with her; surgical mask and droplet precautions.
  4. Communicate: ISBAR to the ED; letter with drug, dose and time; explain to Molly and her mum.
  5. Public health: notify the public health unit urgently by phone.

• CSF: bacterial: neutrophils 8500, protein 1.1, glucose ratio 0.24. Gram-negative diplococci and PCR detected: N. meningitidis; culture no growth to date, most likely from the pre-hospital antibiotic.
  • Molly: IV ceftriaxone 2 g 12-hourly, 5 days in total; no separate clearance antibiotic needed.
  • Public health (already notified on suspicion): confirm they have the laboratory result; they lead contact tracing.
  • Contacts: her parents and tent-mates (household-like, 7 days before onset): a clearance antibiotic as soon as possible (one regimen, e.g. ciprofloxacin); MenACWY if serogroup A, C, W or Y.
  • Contacts' red flags: fever, severe headache, stiff neck, vomiting, drowsiness, or spots or bruises that don't fade: call 000 or go straight to the ED.
  • Molly after discharge: a formal hearing test, GP review of her recovery, and a check of her meningococcal vaccination.

ddx.dx: Bacterial meningitis due to Neisseria meningitidis (meningococcal meningitis)
ddx.for: Fever of 39 °C, a worsening generalised headache, neck stiffness, photophobia and a positive Kernig's sign in an 18-year-old after a crowded festival with a shared tent and uncertain meningococcal vaccination; the CSF is neutrophilic with a low glucose, Gram-negative diplococci and a positive N. meningitidis PCR.
A coryzal prodrome in a young adult who is alert with no focal signs, after mixing with large crowds.
ddx.against: The CSF has 8500 neutrophils, a protein of 1.1 g/L, a glucose ratio of 0.24 and Gram-negative diplococci.

ddx.for: A throbbing headache with photophobia that is worse with movement.
ddx.against: It is her first headache like this, with fever, neck stiffness and a positive Kernig's sign, and no aura, nausea or previous attacks.

ddx.dx: Influenza or another viral respiratory illness
ddx.for: A runny nose 3 days ago, then fever, aches and malaise after crowds.
ddx.against: She has neck stiffness and a positive Kernig's sign, which a simple viral illness does not explain.
She is alert and oriented (GCS 15) with no seizures, behaviour change or focal signs, and the CSF is neutrophilic with organisms seen.

ddx.for: A severe headache with photophobia and neck stiffness.
ddx.against: The headache built up over hours, she has a fever and a coryzal prodrome, and the CSF has no xanthochromia and only 5 red cells.

guide:
Part 1:

  • Give the findings from the Exam findings only when the candidate says what they are examining. The observations are given as values in Part 1, and the repeat set is handed over in Part 2.
  • Molly gives the fever, neck stiffness, photophobia and runny nose only when each is asked about. She says she has no rash only if asked.
  • Item 9: credit each cluster that is asked about.
  • If the candidate stops in Part 1 to say they would call an ambulance and give antibiotics now, say “Noted, please continue,” and credit items 30 and 31 in Part 2 if they repeat them there. This is the right instinct.
  • Molly's mum is not played.

Part 2 (staged):

  • Hand over the observations and ask questions 1 to 3. Molly asks her two questions during the management answer (question 3).
  • Then hand over the CSF and blood results, give Molly's question (“Is it meningococcal? Are Mum and my friends going to catch it?”) as the lead-in, and ask question 4. The hospital results did not exist when Molly was in the practice, so do not expect them in the ISBAR or the first diagnosis answer.
  • Score item 25 from question 1. Score item 33 from question 1 (the letter may be credited in question 3). Score items 26 and 27 from question 2, and items 30, 31, 32 and 34 from question 3.
  • Credit item 36 in question 3 (or in question 1 if stated in the Recommendation).
  • Question 4 carries five marks: items 28.1, 28.2, 35, 37 and 39. The bloods, the absence of xanthochromia and the doses of each clearance regimen are credit only, not required. Credit item 35 if the candidate states the ceftriaxone plan (5 days in total, no separate clearance antibiotic) in question 3 or question 4. Item 40 is not scored.

High-performing candidate: establishes a gradual-onset headache with fever, neck stiffness and photophobia. They ask directly about a rash, allergies and vaccination, and find out who Molly shared a tent with. They examine for meningism, inspect the whole skin and check for focal signs and papilloedema. In Part 2 they recognise worsening suspected sepsis and give ceftriaxone or benzylpenicillin straight away, call 000, notify public health and hand over clearly. They read the CSF as bacterial meningitis caused by N. meningitidis and plan clearance antibiotics for her parents and tent-mates through public health, with red flags for the contacts and a clear instruction to call 000 or go to the ED.

Borderline candidate: takes a generic headache history without asking about fever, rash or the neck. They are reassured by the absence of a rash, or send her to hospital without an antibiotic or in the family car. They wait for a CT or LP before treating, misread the CSF as viral, or forget the contacts.
explain:
Fever and headache: think of meningitis first

A headache with fever, neck stiffness and photophobia is bacterial meningitis until proven otherwise. The classic picture (fever, neck stiffness and an altered conscious state) is often incomplete, and Molly is fully alert. A rash is absent in many people with meningococcal meningitis, and in septicaemia it may appear only later, so no rash does not mean no meningococcal disease. Always ask about a rash and look over the whole skin. Explain why you are asking, because the family may not have looked.

The rest of the headache history rules out the other causes in clusters:

  • Subarachnoid haemorrhage: a thunderclap onset (hers built up over hours).
  • Encephalitis: confusion, behaviour change, seizures, focal signs (none).
  • Raised pressure or tumour: vomiting, focal deficits, a progressive course over weeks (none).
  • Primary headaches: migraine (previous attacks, aura), cluster (one-sided with a red, watering eye), tension-type (band-like) and trigeminal neuralgia (triggered, shock-like facial pain) do not fit a first, febrile headache with meningism.
  • Giant cell arteritis: does not occur at 18.

Why meningococcal disease

Neisseria meningitidis spreads through close and prolonged contact with respiratory secretions. Adolescents and young adults are a peak age group. Crowded living (such as sharing a tent), intimate kissing and smoking increase carriage and spread. Molly is 18, has just come back from a three-day festival where she shared a tent with three friends, had a coryzal prodrome, and is not sure whether she had the meningococcal ACWY (adolescent school program) or B vaccines.

The observations

Fever, tachycardia and tachypnoea with a suspected CNS infection mean suspected sepsis, and she is getting worse even over 15 minutes. Her BP is maintained, her perfusion is normal and she is alert, so she is not yet shocked. On the NSW adult Between the Flags chart, HR and temperature in both sets, and RR in the repeat set, sit in the yellow zone (RR 24 at 10:20 is just below the yellow band of 25–29; check the current CEC version of the chart). In a GP room, suspected sepsis with meningism is an emergency.

Management in general practice (eTG; CDNA guidelines)

  • Antibiotic first: for suspected meningococcal disease outside hospital, give benzylpenicillin 2.4 g IV or IM (eTG adult dose; accept 1.2 g per CDNA) or ceftriaxone 2 g IV or IM immediately. The CDNA guidelines list a pre-hospital benzylpenicillin dose of 1.2 g for adults and children aged 10 years and over. (For children, eTG gives benzylpenicillin 60 mg/kg up to 2.4 g.) Do not delay the antibiotic for blood cultures, the ambulance or tests. Check for allergy first.
  • Transfer: call 000 for an ambulance; do not send her in a private car. Phone the ED with an ISBAR handover, and send a letter with the drug, dose and time.
  • While waiting: IV access, repeat observations, oxygen if hypoxic and a fluid bolus if shock develops. Use droplet precautions.
  • Notify: meningococcal disease is urgently notifiable. Phone the public health unit as soon as it is suspected, without waiting for confirmation.

In hospital: cultures, CT and lumbar puncture

Blood cultures are taken and IV ceftriaxone 2 g 12-hourly is given (continued, if ceftriaxone was the pre-hospital antibiotic). Dexamethasone 10 mg IV 6-hourly is given ideally before or with the first antibiotic dose. Molly had a pre-hospital dose, so the ED team decides on starting it according to eTG and local guidance. Stop it if a non-pneumococcal organism is confirmed, because its benefit is shown mainly in pneumococcal meningitis. A CT before the LP is needed only if she has a reduced or fluctuating conscious state, focal signs, seizures, papilloedema or immunocompromise; Molly has none of these. Imaging must never delay antibiotics.

Consent for the LP:

  • Indication: to confirm meningitis and identify the organism.
  • Procedure: she lies on her side; local anaesthetic is given; a needle is passed between the lower lumbar vertebrae; three samples are collected.
  • Benefits: a firm diagnosis and the right antibiotic.
  • Risks: headache and bruising; rarely, infection or nerve injury.
  • Alternatives: blood cultures and PCR, which are less accurate.
  • Contraindications: signs of raised intracranial pressure, infection of the skin over the site, coagulopathy, and shock.
  • Documentation: record the consent.

Molly's CSF fits the bacterial pattern on every measure:

  • Bacterial pattern: turbid, raised opening pressure, 8500 neutrophils, protein 1.1 g/L and a glucose ratio of 0.24 (1.2/5.0).
  • Organism: Gram-negative diplococci on Gram stain and a positive N. meningitidis PCR. The culture has no growth to date, most likely because the antibiotic was given before the LP: pre-hospital antibiotics often sterilise cultures, so PCR confirms the diagnosis.
  • Not a bleed: no xanthochromia and only 5 red cells.

Her bloods show a bacterial inflammatory response (WCC 21.6, neutrophils 19.2, CRP 168) and a mildly raised lactate (2.4). Normal platelets and clotting show no DIC, but she remains septic and needs close monitoring.

Treatment: IV ceftriaxone 2 g 12-hourly is the treatment for meningococcal meningitis, for a total duration of 5 days. Ceftriaxone clears nasopharyngeal carriage, so on ceftriaxone Molly needs no separate clearance antibiotic. If the isolate is penicillin-susceptible, benzylpenicillin 2.4 g IV 4-hourly is an alternative, but then Molly needs a clearance antibiotic before discharge.

Public health and close contacts (CDNA Series of National Guidelines: Invasive meningococcal disease)

The public health unit, notified when the disease was first suspected, leads the response once it has the laboratory confirmation.

  • Who counts as a close contact: household and household-like contacts in the 7 days before onset (her parents, and the friends who shared her tent) and intimate kissing contacts. The public health unit decides on anyone else. Sharing drinks, cigarettes or utensils, or being at the same festival, does not on its own make someone a close contact.
  • Clearance antibiotics: given as soon as possible to all close contacts. Adult options are ciprofloxacin 500 mg orally once, ceftriaxone 250 mg IM once, or rifampicin 600 mg orally 12-hourly for 2 days.
  • Vaccine: MenACWY vaccine for close contacts if the serogroup is A, C, W or Y; MenB vaccine for contacts only if the public health unit advises it.
  • Warning: contacts are told that clearance antibiotics do not fully remove the risk. Fever, a severe headache, a stiff neck, vomiting, drowsiness or a rash mean ED or 000 straight away.

Follow-up

After discharge, Molly should see her GP:

  • Hearing test: a formal test, because bacterial meningitis can cause sensorineural hearing loss.
  • Recovery: a check on her headache, fatigue, concentration and mood, and on her return to study.
  • Vaccination: her meningococcal vaccination status checked on the Australian Immunisation Register and updated as the Australian Immunisation Handbook advises.
points: Fever, headache, neck stiffness and photophobia mean bacterial meningitis until proven otherwise. Ask about and look for a rash, but its absence does not exclude meningococcal disease.

Screen the other causes of headache in clusters: thunderclap onset (SAH), confusion or seizures (encephalitis), vomiting and focal signs (raised pressure), and the features of migraine, cluster and tension-type headache.

In general practice, for suspected meningococcal disease in an adult, give benzylpenicillin 2.4 g IV or IM (eTG adult dose; accept 1.2 g per CDNA) or ceftriaxone 2 g IV or IM immediately and call 000. Never delay the antibiotic for cultures, imaging or the ambulance.

A CT before LP is needed only for a reduced conscious state, focal signs, seizures, papilloedema or immunocompromise. A neutrophilic CSF with high protein and a glucose ratio below 0.4 is bacterial, and Gram-negative diplococci mean Neisseria meningitidis.

Meningococcal disease is urgently notifiable on suspicion. Public health arranges clearance antibiotics (ciprofloxacin, ceftriaxone or rifampicin) for household and household-like contacts such as tent-mates, and MenACWY vaccine if the serogroup is A, C, W or Y; contacts should still call 000 or go to the ED for fever, headache or a rash.
After bacterial meningitis, arrange a formal hearing test and GP follow-up, and update meningococcal vaccination.
